question.problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
\mathbf T(t) =\sin{t} \,\mathbf i -\cos{t}\,\mathbf j.
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that in general, the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}‖i+j‖ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)}{1}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

To check our result, we can verify that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ are perpendicular by computing their dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
